subject: Computer Science
topic: Growth rates, nested loops and choosing a data structure
scope: Original shared study module on growth rates, nested loops and choosing a data structure. Numerical datasets and quoted passages are invented teaching examples. This is not a complete course, official examination material or verified board-specific alignment.
prerequisites: Trace a loop and count iterations.
objectives: Count work in sequential and nested loops.
Distinguish asymptotic growth from measured runtime.
Match a data structure to required operations.

notes.heading: Count the operations that depend on input size
paragraphs: Let n describe the input size and choose a basic operation such as a comparison. A loop with n iterations and constant work per iteration takes a number of operations proportional to n. Two consecutive such loops still have linear growth, because their counts add. A nested pair with n iterations each instead performs n squared combinations when the inner loop runs fully for every outer iteration. Read the bounds carefully: dependent inner bounds, early exits and changing step sizes can alter the count. State which case is being analysed.

notes.heading: Growth is not a stopwatch result
paragraphs: Big-O describes an asymptotic upper bound on growth, not an exact number of seconds. Constants, hardware, implementation and input distribution can change measured runtime. A logarithmic search may require a sorted collection and an efficient way to access its middle element; the cost of preparing that collection belongs in the overall workflow when relevant. Distinguish worst-case, average-case and best-case claims. A test on one small input cannot establish an asymptotic result, although it may expose a bug in a proposed counting argument.

notes.heading: Select structures using required operations
paragraphs: A stack offers last-in-first-out access, while a queue offers first-in-first-out access. Choosing between them depends on the behaviour required, not which name sounds faster. An array can support direct indexed access, but inserting at its beginning may require shifting many entries. A linked representation can change links efficiently when the relevant node is already known, yet finding that node may still require traversal. Include search, insertion, removal and memory constraints when comparing designs. State implementation assumptions rather than claiming that one structure is always faster.

workedExamples.prompt: One loop performs 3n operations and a following loop performs 5n+2. Describe the total and its growth.
steps: For large n the fixed term does not change the linear order of growth.
workedExamples.answer: 8n+2 operations in this count; O(n) growth.

workedExamples.prompt: For each i from 1 through n, a loop performs i operations. Find the count when n=4 and its general form.
steps: In general the sum is n(n+1)/2, which has quadratic growth.

misconceptions.claim: Every pair of loops is quadratic.
misconceptions.correction: Consecutive loops add; nesting and bounds determine multiplication.

misconceptions.claim: An O(n) algorithm always beats an O(n²) one for every n.
misconceptions.correction: Constants and input size can affect finite runtime comparisons.

questions.prompt: A loop visits n items twice, followed by a fixed 7 operations. Give the exact count and order under this model.
solution: Add the two visits per item and fixed work.
Retain the highest growth term for the asymptotic order.

questions.prompt: For i=1,...,6, an inner loop executes i times. How many inner iterations occur?
Tasks A, B and C enter a queue in that order. After one removal, D joins. Give the remaining removal order.
solution: A leaves first by first-in-first-out behaviour.
D joins behind B and C.

questions.prompt: One search is required in an unsorted list. A learner ignores sorting cost and claims binary search is automatically the best whole workflow. Explain the missing consideration.
questions.answer: Sorting and access costs must be included; a single linear scan may be preferable.
solution: Binary search's logarithmic comparison count assumes suitable sorted input.
Compare the total preparation-plus-search work for the actual number of searches.
markingPoints: Compare total rather than isolated search cost.
